newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Posco steals show.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Posco steals show.

text.p: A Yankee for South Korea's Posco was the major issue in Asian debt markets on Wednesday, but other issuers also came through with big deals.
As expected, South Korea's Pohang Iron and Steel launched a US$300 million 10-year note into the U.S. Yankee market via lead manager Salomon Brothers.
The 7.125 percent notes were launched at 99.887 to yield 7.141 percent or 70 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries.
The spread was a bit narrower than expected and a lot skinnier than the pricing on Posco's last Yankee. The company launched a 10-year bond in May 1995 that paid 90 basis points over the benchmark.
The bonds reportedly were all sold, but dealers said the issue's success will not be determined until it is free to trade in the secondary market.
One trader said he expected the notes to trade in the low 70s once the deal is freed, which would be about 15 basis wider than bonds of the South Korean quasi-sovereigns.
Hanil Bank brought its US$200 million FRN. The three-year paper pays a coupon of 21 basis points over the London Interbank Offered Rate and an all-in return of about 26 basis points to the top tier.
Bankers said the pricing was about right.
The underwriters, Fuji International Finance (HK), Barclays de Zoete Wedd, Lehman Brothers, LTCB ASia and Sanwa International Finance, kept the entire issue.
First Bangkok City Bank launched a US$100 million floating rate certificate of deposit issue. The certificates have a three-year final maturity and can be put at 99.95 after two years.
They pay a margin of 42.5 basis points over LIBOR and an all-in return of 67.5 basis points.
That's wider than the bank's last issue launched in July, which paid 50 basis points to the top tier.
Bankers cited several reasons for the wider pricing.

Moody's Investors Service's downgrading of Thailand's short-term debt has hurt Thai paper in the secondary market, and the proximity to the year's end means that many banks already have filled their books with as much Thai paper as they want.
Also, "the other deal was a bit tight," said one banker.
In other news, Tri Polyta BV, a unit of Tri Polyta Indonesia, has filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission to offer U.S. investors up to US$175 million in guaranteed notes due 2003.
The offering will be made through Merrill Lynch, Lehman Brothers and Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp.
Proceeds will be used by Tri Polyta to refinance debt and to make investments in certain petrochemical projects.
